name: Hypocognition
statement: People identify and remember less of what they have no concept for, a gap Robert Levy named hypocognition.
meaning: Hypocognition is the absence of a concept, not the absence of a thing. Robert Levy used the idea of Tahitian emotion talk, where his informants had no settled term for what he took to be sadness. Kaidi Wu and David Dunning carried it into psychology and defined it as lacking a schema, meaning a knowledge structure holding a concept's features and the associations between them. Someone hypocognitive of a durian can look straight at the fruit and still fail to encode it, having nowhere to file what they saw. Wu and Dunning pair the term with hypercognition, the overapplication of a concept a person does have to matters it does not fit. The claim concerns the shape of attention and memory rather than a motivated error, which sets it apart from most of the entries here.

origin.where: Tahitians: Mind and Experience in the Society Islands, University of Chicago Press
origin.note: Levy's book runs to 547 pages and was not read for this entry, so the attribution rests on two later sources. Wu and Dunning credit the coinage to Levy in 1973. Jason Throop, writing in Ethos in 2005, quotes Levy's phrase 'hypocognized emotions' from page 287 and his account of Tahitian responses to loss from page 305. Both quote the adjective. Whether the noun hypocognition itself appears in the 1973 text was not established here.

evidence: The paper everyone cites carries no data. Wu and Dunning's 2018 article in Review of General Psychology is a review, and the abstract deposited with Crossref says so in its second sentence. The experiments sit in an unpublished manuscript the same two authors posted to PsyArXiv in October 2019, six studies with 2,085 participants. Study 1 put 20 unfamiliar concepts to 302 American adults, among them benevolent sexism and vocal fry, and asked how often they had met each over the previous two weeks. People who did not know a concept reported fewer encounters with it, b = 0.82, 95% confidence interval 0.53 to 1.10, t(78.85) = 5.92, p < .001. Study 2A showed 212 Americans a basket of five common and five exotic fruits for ten seconds, then tested recognition after a two-minute distraction task. Sensitivity was d' = 1.38 for the familiar fruits and 0.79 for the unfamiliar ones. Studies 3 and 4 moved to counting. Shown fruits or foods at set frequencies, 196 Americans tracked exotic fruits less well than common ones, and in Study 4 the 189 British participants tracked cheese better than dumplings, slope 0.40 against 0.21, while the 212 Chinese participants showed the reverse. Study 5 gave 702 Americans rotated cursive letters accompanied by no sound, a nonsense sound, or the sound the letter makes. A nonsense label helped less than a label carrying the concept, interaction b = 0.05, standard error 0.02, p = .023, which is the authors' evidence that hypocognition is more than a missing word. Their 2020 chapter applies the idea to what men and white Americans fail to generate and recall about discrimination, and describes those studies in prose with no figures attached.

replication.headline: No independent test of the hypocognition experiments was found: the six studies remain an unpublished 2019 preprint, and the three works Semantic Scholar records as citing it include the authors' own book chapter.

limits: Nobody outside the two authors has been found to have run the studies. The search, on 10 August 2026, covered a Crossref bibliographic query for hypocognition, which returns seven records, three of them by Wu and Dunning; the Semantic Scholar citation lists for the 2018 review and the 2019 preprint; and open web searches for replications and critiques. The 39 papers citing the review apply the term across nursing education, ecological modelling, philosophy and accounting history rather than testing it. Several caveats attach to the preprint itself. It has not been peer reviewed, it was last modified in May 2020, it mentions no preregistration, and its supplemental materials, which hold the sample-size rules and the exclusion criteria for all six studies, were not obtained. One passage does not hold together: the frequency slopes reported for Chinese participants, 0.30 for cheese and 0.41 for dumplings, carry intervals of 0.36 to 0.46 and 0.26 to 0.34, and neither interval brackets its own estimate. On the anthropology, Levy's book was not opened, and his 1984 chapter 'Emotion, knowing, and culture' was not obtained. The widely repeated claim that Levy tied the Tahitian hypocognition of grief to the islands' suicide rate appears in no source read here and is left out. Kaidi Wu's essay in Aeon and the Scientific American piece she wrote with Dunning were both unreachable during this task.
misreadings: The commonest error is that a missing word makes a feeling impossible. Levy's page 305, as quoted by Throop, says his informants had 'no unambiguous terms which represent the concepts of sadness, longing, or loneliness', and that they named their state as feeling troubled, heavy or fatigued. Wu and Dunning write that Tahitians experienced facets of grief privately and lacked any shared acknowledgement of it. The claim is about naming and noticing, not about the capacity to feel. The second error is treating the idea as a vocabulary problem, which Study 5 was designed to rule out: a nonsense label attached to an unfamiliar symbol helped less than a label carrying the concept. The third is quotation drift. Wu and Dunning's chapter says Tahitians described their sorrow as feeling 'sick' or 'strange', which is not the set of terms Throop quotes from page 305, and retellings pick one wording or the other without saying which text they follow. The fourth is the word bias. Hypocognition names a gap in knowledge rather than a slanted judgement, and Wu and Dunning's own framing is one of expertise, in which a person without a concept is a novice about it. The fifth is citing the 2018 review as the source of the experiments. It reviews other people's work and reports none of its own.

sources.text: Wu, K., & Dunning, D. (2018). Hypocognition: Making Sense of the Landscape beyond One's Conceptual Reach. Review of General Psychology, 22(1), 25-35. A review article. Its abstract was read from the publisher's deposit at Crossref; the full text is closed at SAGE and was not obtained.

Wu, K., & Dunning, D. (2019). Hypocognitive Mind: How Lack of Conceptual Knowledge Confines What People See and Remember. Unpublished manuscript posted to PsyArXiv on 17 October 2019. Source of every study figure quoted above; the PDF was downloaded from OSF and read in full.

Wu, K., & Dunning, D. (2020). Hypocognition and the Invisibility of Social Privilege. Advances in Group Processes, 37, 1-23. Emerald. Source of the schema definition and of the authors' attribution of the term to Levy; read from a PDF copy hosted by SciSpace.

Throop, C. J. (2005). Hypocognition, a 'Sense of the Uncanny,' and the Anthropology of Ambiguity: Reflections on Robert I. Levy's Contribution to Theories of Experience in Anthropology. Ethos, 33(4), 499-511. Source of the Levy quotations at pages 285, 287 and 305, which are therefore quoted here at one remove.

Open Library catalogue record for Levy, R. I. (1973). Tahitians: mind and experience in the Society Islands. University of Chicago Press, 547 pages. Used to confirm the title, subtitle, publisher, year and length. The book itself was not read.
